newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle Columbia moved to launch pad.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle Columbia moved to launch pad.

text.p: The U.S. space shuttle Columbia was moved to its launch pad on Wednesday for a rerun of a mission cut short in April by mechanical trouble.
A giant tracked transporter hauled Columbia the 3.4 miles (5.4 km) from its assembly building to the launch pad on Wednesday morning in preparation for the planned July 1 blast off.
The shuttle and its crew of seven astronauts were to repeat a mission curtailed after only five days because of trouble with an electrical generator.
It was only the third time a shuttle flight had ended early due to mechanical problems. The microgravity research mission was to have lasted 16 days.
Columbia was readied in near-record time for its second try at the truncated mission. The shuttle spent only 56 days being prepared in its hangar, compared with the usual 85.
The discovery of some cracked insulation tiles and others prone to similar damage on the shuttle's nose has left the space agency scrambling to complete launch preparations.
"The schedule we have laid out says we can meet the July 1 launch date, but it's very tight," NASA spokesman Joel Wells said.
Dozens of tiles, which protect the shuttle from the searing heat of reentry into Earth's atmosphere, are being replaced with stronger material.
Weather permitting, the repair work should be completed just hours before the shuttle's three-day countdown starts on June 28.
About 40 tiles will also need replacing on each of Columbia's three sister ships, Atlantis, Discovery and Endeavour.
